text: You have a chosen model and a sealed test set. This final lesson does three things — evaluates the model honestly, adds an unsupervised lens with clustering, and turns the whole project into something you can show an employer. It's also the last lesson of the course, so we finish with a look at what you can now do.

The model and every choice were fixed using training data only. Now we score the test set exactly once: ROC AUC comes out to 0.807, accuracy about 0.74. Of 262 customers who stayed, the model correctly cleared 229 and wrongly flagged 33. Of 138 who churned, it caught 68 and missed 70.

Compared with the baseline — 0.5 AUC, 0.655 accuracy — the model clearly learned something real. The test AUC of 0.807 sits a bit above the cross-validated 0.776, and with only 400 test rows, some variation is expected. Report the test number, but never go back and adjust the model to chase a better one.

At the default 0.5 cutoff, recall on churners is only about half — the threshold is actually a business decision. Dropping it to 0.4 raises recall from 0.493 to 0.681 while precision only falls slightly, though the outreach list grows from 101 to 148 customers. At 0.3, recall reaches 0.812 with a list of 201. Present the options and let the business pick.

Supervised models answer who will leave. Clustering asks what kinds of customers do we have. Running k-means on the three numeric features across k of 2 through 6: the silhouette scores are low and flat, 0.293 down to 0.252 — no sharply separated natural groups, unlike the clean blobs of earlier lessons. That's normal for real business data.

Choosing k equals 3 for interpretability and profiling the segments: segment 1 is long-tenured, loyal customers, churning at just 0.14. Segment 0 is newer customers with few support calls, churning at 0.35. Segment 2 is newer customers who call support often, churning at 0.46 — the group to prioritize for proactive outreach.

A strong portfolio project says what it cannot claim. The data is synthetic, so real-world performance is unknown. The model finds associations, not causes — autopay correlating with lower churn doesn't prove enabling it retains customers. There's no time dimension, and the test set's 400 rows carry meaningful uncertainty.

Package the repository with a README covering the problem, data, approach, results, threshold recommendation, segments, and limitations — employers want to see your thinking, not just your code. Present it as a story in five to seven slides, leading with the decision the audience must make, not the algorithm.

You can now frame a prediction problem, split and prepare data without leakage, build linear, tree-based, and instance-based models, group and compress data with clustering and PCA, evaluate with the right metrics, and communicate the result. The next course, Applied Machine Learning, takes these ideas into a production-minded workflow — tuning, imbalanced and messy data, and applied projects.
